summary: Content-Centric Networking uses delta time values in several places. For constrained nodes or low-bandwidth networks, a compact encoding helps, which requires trading accuracy against range. This experimental document specifies a logarithmic encoding using compact floating-point arithmetic. It updates RFC 8609.

eli5.summary: Instead of writing every digit of a time, it writes it in a short "number times power" form, the way big numbers are shortened in science.

questions: what is ccnx compact time encoding
how does the ccnx time code work
what does rfc 9510 change in rfc 8609
subtitle: A one-byte logarithmic time code that shrinks CCNx Interest Lifetime and Recommended Cache Time for constrained networks.

tldr.problem: CCNx encodes the Interest Lifetime as a 64-bit integer, which is wasteful in low-power, bandwidth-constrained networks. Any compact time representation must trade accuracy against range.
tldr.mechanism: A one-byte time code holds a 5-bit exponent and a 3-bit mantissa, giving a logarithmic range from milliseconds to years. A TLV with Length = 1 now carries this code for Interest Lifetime and Recommended Cache Time.
tldr.outcome: This Experimental RFC updates RFC 8609. Mixed networks of updated and legacy forwarders need care, since a legacy forwarder reads the code as a plain number of milliseconds or as an absolute time.

today: RFC 9510 is an Experimental RFC from the IRTF that updates RFC 8609. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Compress Time Values
sections.content:
Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) uses absolute and delta time values for several functions. In resource-constrained environments, such as the bandwidth-constrained IEEE 802.15.4 deployments that motivated this work, a compact representation of time is valuable. But any compact representation has to give up accuracy or dynamic range.

RFC 9510 is a product of the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group. It discusses the various uses of time values, proposes a compact encoding for delta times, and updates RFC 8609 to use it in CCNx messages. It does not constitute an IETF standard.
sections.eli5: Sending a long number on a tiny, slow connection is like mailing a whole book when a postcard would do. This document shows how to write the time on a postcard.

sections.title: Where CCNx Uses Time
sections.content:
CCNx uses relative time (delta time) only for the lifetime of an Interest message. That value is hop-by-hop and is currently encoded by the T_INTLIFE TLV as a 64-bit integer. Every Interest is expected to carry it in all but some corner cases, so a compact form keeps Interests short.

CCNx also uses absolute time. Signature Time (T_SIGTIME) and Expiry Time (T_EXPIRY) are 64-bit timestamps in milliseconds since the POSIX epoch, and they sit inside the message's security envelope. The RFC concludes there is no practical compact encoding that preserves their meaning and security, so it does not touch them.

The Recommended Cache Time (T_CACHETIME) is also a 64-bit absolute time in milliseconds. It cannot be in the past and is likely a short offset from now, so this document lets it be read as a relative value when the compact representation is used.
sections.eli5: Some times are like 'wait five minutes' and some are like 'be there at exactly 3:15 on Tuesday'. Only the 'wait this long' kind can be shortened without breaking anything.

sections.title: The One-Byte Time Code
sections.content:
The time code packs an exponent (5 bits) and a mantissa (3 bits) into one byte. There is no sign bit, because only non-negative values are encoded. The base unit is seconds, and with a constant C = 1/32 the value is computed as follows.

  • Subnormal, exponent b = 0: (0 + a/8) * 2 * C
  • Normalized, exponent b > 0: (1 + a/8) * 2^b * C

Here a is the mantissa. The subnormal form gives gradual underflow: eight values in the range [0s, ~0.0546875s] with a step of ~0.0078125s. The scale runs from milliseconds to years, with finer precision for small values.

Not every time can be represented. The example encoding algorithm produces the code closest to, and smaller than, the input. For instance, 0.063 maps to exponent 1 and mantissa 0, the same as 0.0625.
sections.eli5: It is like writing big numbers in science style: a few digits plus a power. Small amounts get tiny steps, and enormous amounts get giant steps, all inside one byte.

sections.title: Changes to Interest Lifetime and Cache Time
sections.content:
The RFC signals the new encoding with a 1-byte length field while keeping the existing TLV registry entries. It admits this has backward-compatibility problems, but argues it is acceptable: both CCNx RFCs are Experimental, the main use is smaller IoT and sensor networks, and these TLVs are hop-by-hop and not covered by a signed hash, so a forwarder supporting the new encoding can translate freely between the two.

For the Interest Lifetime, a value of length 1 used to be a linear range [0,255] in milliseconds. It is now always a compact time code. Other lengths follow RFC 8609. For the Recommended Cache Time, a value of length 1 is now a compact relative time code, and other lengths stay absolute 8-byte times. A node turns the relative code into absolute time using the reception time, and computes a fresh code on transmission.

An appendix gives a cheaper approximation for forwarders, using bit shifts, with an error of 2.4%.
sections.eli5: A one-byte note now means 'this is the short code'. Old notes stay as they were. Because these notes only matter between neighbours, each router can rewrite them in whichever style the next one understands.

sections.title: Security and Mixed Networks
sections.content:
The document makes no semantic changes to CCNx or to the security properties of its message encodings, so it has the same security considerations as RFC 8569 and RFC 8609. The concern is networks that mix updated and legacy forwarders.

For Interest Lifetime, a legacy forwarder reads the code as 0 to 255 milliseconds, so Pending Interest Table entries may time out sooner than expected. An updated forwarder reading a short lifetime set by a legacy forwarder may configure timeouts of up to 4 years, which wastes state space.

For Recommended Cache Time, a legacy forwarder treats a length-1 value as a syntax error and SHOULD discard the packet. Otherwise it reads the code as an absolute time far in the past, which hurts cache use. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If an old router reads the new short code, it gets the wrong idea about how long to wait. It might give up too fast, or a new router might hold on far too long. That is why mixing old and new needs care.

fields.name: Exponent (b)
fields.desc: Power-of-two scale of the time value.
